4
What is a typical value of the wavelength of a microwave travelling in a vacuum?
A
3 000 000 pm
B
30 nm
C
30 000 µm
D
3000 mm

hints: Recall where microwaves sit in the electromagnetic spectrum - between infrared with wavelengths near $1\text{ mm}$ and radio waves with wavelengths near $1\text{ m}$.
Convert each prefix to metres: $1\text{ pm}=10^{-12}\text{ m}$, $1\text{ nm}=10^{-9}\text{ m}$, $1\text{ }\mu\text{m}=10^{-6}\text{ m}$, $1\text{ mm}=10^{-3}\text{ m}$.
Check which of $3\,000\,000\text{ pm}$, $30\text{ nm}$, $30\,000\text{ }\mu\text{m}$ and $3000\text{ mm}$ gives a few centimetres, about $10^{-2}\text{ m}$.
walkthrough: Microwaves are part of the electromagnetic spectrum with typical wavelengths from about $1\text{ mm} = 10^{-3}\text{ m}$ to about $1\text{ m}$.
Convert each option to metres using standard prefixes to compare with that range.
Option A: $3\,000\,000\text{ pm} = 3 \times 10^{6} \times 10^{-12}\text{ m} = 3 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}$. Option B: $30\text{ nm} = 30 \times 10^{-9}\text{ m} = 3.0 \times 10^{-8}\text{ m}$.
Option C: $30\,000\text{ }\mu\text{m} = 3 \times 10^{4} \times 10^{-6}\text{ m} = 3.0 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m} = 3\text{ cm}$. Option D: $3000\text{ mm} = 3000 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m} = 3.0\text{ m}$.
Only $3.0 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$ lies inside the $10^{-3}\text{ m}$ to $1\text{ m}$ microwave band. The others are infrared, ultraviolet and radio wave respectively. This is option C.

A.explanation: $3\,000\,000\text{ pm} = 3 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}$, which is a few micrometres and typical of infrared, not microwaves.

B.explanation: $30\text{ nm} = 3.0 \times 10^{-8}\text{ m}$, which is in the ultraviolet region and far too short for a microwave.

C.explanation: $30\,000\text{ }\mu\text{m} = 3.0 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m} = 3\text{ cm}$, which lies in the typical $1\text{ mm}$ to $1\text{ m}$ microwave band.

D.explanation: $3000\text{ mm} = 3.0\text{ m}$, which is in the radio-wave region and too long for a typical microwave.
